title: Joining Eddie Condon's band and its rhythm section
summary: Condon hires Leeman, letting him send subs on Saturdays; he praises Gene Schroeder, Bob Casey and Walter Page, whom he recommended, and Condon's unamplified guitar.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: But I was approached by Eddie Condon who said why aren't you at Nick's, and I said they wouldn't let me off on Saturday night for a couple hours so I could do my Hit Parade, which I was just starting to do. Record dates in New York, and everybody was recognizing me, because I'm on the Hit Parade.

And he said, did I want to come down, because he needed a drummer, and I think it was George Wettling's place that I took -- and I said yes, and he said you can take off on Saturdays and you send somebody that can play, because they were never satisfied, I don't know, a funny bunch of people they were -- they weren't satisfied with any subs I'd send, but anyway, he said to take off whenever I wanted, as long as you sent somebody that was capable to take your place. And that's how I went over to Eddie Condon's, and all of a sudden, I was working with one of the greatest bands in its category that I ever worked with -- and that's the Chicago, windy, Chicago style, jazz straight down the middle.

But they had an inspiring way of playing that they had worked out because they worked together so long. You know, I had a wonderful rhythm section; we had Gene Schragden on piano, and he's passed away long since.
Our first bass player was Bob Casey, and he had become -- he used to have a drinking problem, and he was on

the wagon trying to make his life, and he couldn't stand being around all the drunks down there, so one of the -- I'll take a pat on the back -- one of my dear, dear friends, I suggested, and Eddie Condon hired him -- was Bigun -- Walter Page.
Who had left Basie long before ... (CUT)
... your dear friend Walter Page, which was part of that great rhythm section known as one of the world's greatest.

I'm not particularly in love with guitars and banjos or anything that get in the way, I love a rhythm section with bass, piano and drums. There's enough configuration going on there. But Eddie Condon is an unsung hero; people never gave him credit for it -- he had a wonderful sense of chord progressions and so forth. He played the guitar, because it was unamplified, and never did get in the way. And it was just a joy to work with him, and all I could do was feel him a little bit here and there; he knew what to do; laid out on the piano.
